_note: Curated, offline knowledge vault. Every entry cites ids from data/sources.json. Content is general guidance written conservatively; always follow local emergency services first.

entries.title: Make a household emergency plan
entries.summary: Agree on contacts, meeting places and who does what before an emergency happens.
points: Write down emergency contacts and keep a paper copy — phones may be flat or networks down.
Choose a meeting place near home and one outside your neighbourhood.
Assign roles: who checks on children, pets, older neighbours, and who collects the kit.
Know how you will receive official warnings (radio, emergency alert apps, local emergency services websites).
Review and practise the plan at least once a year.

entries.title: What goes in an emergency survival kit
entries.summary: Food, water, light, a radio, first aid, medication, documents and chargers in one grab-and-go place.
points: Food and water, torch and batteries, a battery or wind-up radio, a first aid kit and medication.
Mobile phone, chargers and power banks; warm waterproof clothing and sturdy shoes.
Copies of identity, insurance and medical documents in a waterproof bag.
A manual can opener, garbage bags and ties for sanitation, and a whistle to signal for help.
Check the kit regularly and replace expired items.

entries.title: How much water to store and how to store it
entries.summary: Plan at least about 1 US gallon (3.8 L) per person per day; more in heat, for children, nursing mothers and sick people.
points: Store at least ~3.8 L (1 US gallon) per person per day for drinking and sanitation.
Very hot conditions can double water needs; children, nursing mothers and people who are ill may need more.
Unopened commercially bottled water is the safest option; keep it in a cool, dark place.
If filling your own containers, use clean food-grade containers, seal them, label the date and replace periodically.
Don't ration drinking water in a way that causes dehydration — drink what you need today and look for more tomorrow.

entries.title: Making water safe in an emergency
entries.summary: Boiling is the surest method; unscented bleach is a backup. Water contaminated with fuel or chemicals cannot be made safe this way.
points: Follow any boil-water or do-not-drink notice from local authorities first.
Boiling: bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 ft / ~2,000 m), cool, and store covered.
If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through clean cloth before treating.
Unscented household bleach can disinfect water when boiling isn't possible — follow the exact CDC dosing for your bleach strength.
Disinfectants work less well than boiling against some parasites (e.g. Cryptosporidium, Giardia).
Water contaminated with fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfection — find another source.

entries.title: Planning an emergency food supply
entries.summary: Count energy (kcal) and meals, not cans. Store food your household will actually eat and can prepare without power.
points: Plan by energy and meals: a can of vegetables and a can of stew are not the same amount of food.
Choose non-perishable foods that need little or no cooking, water or refrigeration.
Account for allergies, dietary requirements, infants, older people and pets.
Rotate stock: use older items first and note expiry dates.
Include a manual can opener and basic utensils.

entries.title: Food safety when the power goes out
entries.summary: Keep fridge and freezer doors shut: about 4 hours for a fridge, ~48 hours for a full freezer (~24 if half full).
points: A closed refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours.
A full freezer holds temperature for about 48 hours (about 24 hours if half full) if the door stays closed.
Discard perishable food (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers) that has been above 40°F / 4°C for more than 2 hours.
Frozen food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F / 4°C or below can be refrozen, though quality may drop.
Never taste food to decide if it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.

entries.title: Extended blackout: the first hours
entries.summary: Check for danger, stay informed, protect food and medicines, and avoid carbon monoxide and fire risks.
points: Check people first: anyone injured, unwell, or reliant on powered medical equipment needs priority — call emergency services if life is at risk.
Use torches rather than candles to reduce fire risk.
Switch off and unplug appliances to protect them from surges when power returns; leave one light switched on so you know when it's back.
Keep fridge and freezer closed; plan meals from pantry food first.
Listen to a battery or wind-up radio for official updates; conserve phone battery.
Check on neighbours, especially older people and those living alone.

entries.title: Carbon monoxide: generators, heaters and cooking
entries.summary: Never run generators, barbecues, camp stoves or fuel heaters indoors or in garages. CO is invisible and deadly.
points: Never use a generator, charcoal grill, camp stove or other fuel-burning device inside a home, garage, basement or tent — even with doors or windows open.
Keep generators outdoors and at least 20 feet (~6 m) from doors, windows and vents.
Install battery-powered CO alarms where possible.
Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, confusion or sleepiness can be CO poisoning: get everyone into fresh air immediately and call emergency services.

entries.title: Portable generator safety
entries.summary: Run outdoors only, keep dry, and never connect a generator to household wiring unless installed by a licensed electrician.
points: Operate outdoors only, away from doors, windows and vents.
Plug appliances into the generator with suitably rated outdoor extension leads.
Never 'back-feed' power into house wiring — it can kill utility workers and neighbours. A proper transfer switch must be installed by a licensed electrician.
Let the generator cool before refuelling and store fuel safely away from the home.

entries.title: Medicines and powered medical devices in an outage
entries.summary: Plan ahead for medicines that need refrigeration and equipment that needs power.
points: Keep a written list of medications, doses and prescribers in your kit.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist how long refrigerated medicines stay usable without power.
If someone depends on powered medical equipment, have a backup power plan and register with your electricity provider if they offer a life-support register.
If a medical device fails and someone's life is at risk, call emergency services immediately.

entries.title: First aid basics and when to call for help
entries.summary: Make the area safe, call for help early, and get trained. Prometheus is not a substitute for medical care.
points: Check for danger to yourself and others before helping.
Call emergency services (000 in Australia, 911 in the US, 112 in many countries) for serious injury, breathing problems, chest pain, severe bleeding or unconsciousness.
Keep a stocked first aid kit and know where it is.
A recognised first aid course is the best preparation — written guidance cannot replace hands-on training.

entries.title: Hygiene and sanitation without running water
entries.summary: Hand hygiene and safe waste handling prevent illness when water and services are disrupted.
points: Wash hands with soap and safe water, or use hand sanitiser, before eating and after using the toilet.
Garbage bags and plastic ties can line a toilet or bucket for personal sanitation when toilets can't flush.
Store waste sealed and away from living areas, food and water.
Keep toilet paper, wet wipes and feminine hygiene supplies in your kit.

entries.title: Staying warm or cool without power
entries.summary: Choose one room, layer clothing and protect vulnerable people from extreme heat or cold.
points: In cold: gather in one room, close doors and curtains, wear layers and use blankets. Never use outdoor heaters or stoves indoors.
In heat: stay in the coolest part of the home, drink water regularly, use damp cloths, and avoid exertion in the hottest hours.
Infants, older people and people with health conditions are most at risk — check on them often.
Go to a designated relief or cooling/warming centre if conditions become unsafe.

entries.title: Staying informed and in contact
entries.summary: A battery or wind-up radio, charged power banks and a written contact list keep you connected.
points: Use a battery or wind-up radio for official emergency broadcasts.
Keep phones on low-power mode; send short text messages instead of calls when networks are congested.
Keep a paper list of contacts and your household plan.
Check official sources for warnings, for example Emergency WA in Western Australia.

entries.title: About fictional scenarios (zombie apocalypse and friends)
entries.summary: Fictional scenarios are training games. They rehearse real skills, but they are not real-world guidance.
points: Prometheus labels fictional simulations clearly.
Use fiction to practise planning, communication and resource management in a low-stakes way.
In a real emergency, follow official guidance and emergency services, not game logic.

entries.title: Energy: the currency of civilisation
entries.summary: Energy is the capacity to do work. Rebuilding anything starts with understanding how energy is stored, converted and lost.
points: Energy comes in forms: chemical (food, fuel, batteries), kinetic (motion), thermal (heat), radiant (sunlight) and electrical.
Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted — and each conversion loses some as heat.
Power is the rate of energy use: 1 watt = 1 joule per second. Batteries are rated in watt-hours (Wh).
Thinking in energy budgets (how much you have vs. how much you use) is the foundation of every survival and rebuilding decision.

entries.title: Circuits, voltage, current and resistance
entries.summary: Current flows around a closed loop, pushed by voltage and limited by resistance (Ohm's law: V = I × R).
points: Voltage (volts) is the electrical 'push'; current (amps) is the flow of charge; resistance (ohms) opposes flow.
Ohm's law: V = I × R. Power: P = V × I.
A circuit needs a complete loop. Series circuits share one path; parallel circuits split current across branches.
Safe way to learn: simulations (e.g. PhET Circuit Construction Kit) and low-voltage commercial learning kits.

entries.title: How solar electricity works
entries.summary: Photovoltaic cells turn sunlight directly into DC electricity; output depends on sunlight, angle, temperature and shading.
points: Solar panels contain photovoltaic (PV) cells that convert light into direct current (DC) electricity.
Output depends on sunlight intensity, panel angle, shading and temperature — it's zero at night.
Storing solar energy requires batteries and a charge controller to charge them safely.
Portable, certified 'solar generator' kits are the safest starting point for households.

entries.title: Batteries and energy storage
entries.summary: Batteries store chemical energy and release it as DC electricity. Capacity in Wh tells you how long they can run a load.
points: Runtime estimate: battery watt-hours ÷ device watts ≈ hours (real results are lower due to losses).
Different chemistries (alkaline, lead-acid, lithium) have different hazards, lifespans and charging needs.
Damaged, swollen or overheating lithium batteries can catch fire — stop using them and keep them away from flammables.
Never short-circuit a battery: large batteries can deliver enough current to cause burns and fires.

entries.title: Electrical safety fundamentals
entries.summary: Mains electricity can kill. Learn with low-voltage kits; leave mains wiring and fixed installations to licensed electricians.
points: Mains (household) voltage can cause fatal shocks and fires. Never open or modify mains equipment or wiring.
Treat fallen power lines as live: stay well away and report them to emergency services.
Water and electricity don't mix: keep electrical equipment dry.
In Australia, electrical installation work must be done by licensed electricians — check your state regulator (e.g. Building and Energy in WA).
Learning safely: simulations, textbooks and certified low-voltage kits.
